strengths: The paper targets an important limitation of monocular HMR: most methods recover image-aligned bodies but not metric-scale body shape and camera-coordinate translation. Framing this around the camera model and perspective projection is useful and timely.

The proposed camera-ray conditioning is conceptually simple and well motivated: it encodes intrinsics, crop geometry, and bounding-box location in a spatial representation that is easier for a network to consume than raw K and box parameters.

The method is attractive in its simplicity compared with temporal/global-trajectory systems: it is per-frame and does not require a dedicated trajectory module, yet obtains competitive global trajectory numbers on EMDB and Human3.6M.

The ablation against directly concatenating bounding-box plus intrinsics is strong: the ray representation greatly improves PA-MPJPE/MPJPE/PVE on both 3DPW and Human3.6M, supporting the central design choice.

The manuscript includes a useful discussion of scale/depth ambiguity under perspective projection and explicitly acknowledges that metric HMR should aim for reasonable scale rather than a unique absolute reconstruction.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper says it achieves state-of-the-art performance, but Table 2 is worse than WHAM/TRAM for local pose, and Table 3 with Masked-DROID is slightly worse than TRAM on WA-MPJPE and W-MPJPE, tied on RTE, and only better on ERVE. The results are competitive, not clearly state of the art.

The training supervision claim is confusing. The paper repeatedly states that no 3D information or 3D supervision is used, but the method is trained on 3DPW, Human3.6M, and MPI-INF-3DHP and uses pose mimic loss and shape loss. It is not clear whether these are ground-truth SMPL/3D-derived labels, pseudo-labels, or only 2D supervision. This materially affects the novelty and fairness of the claim.

There is a potential technical error or at least a serious notation problem in the cropped intrinsic matrix. Eq. 4 appears to use entries like (f_x - u_bbox)/s and c_x/s, whereas standard crop-resize intrinsics should scale focal length and shift the principal point according to the crop origin. Since the whole method depends on ray construction, this needs to be correct and reproducible.

Evaluation protocol details are insufficient. It is unclear when ground-truth intrinsics versus UniDepth-predicted intrinsics are used, whether training/test splits avoid overlap for datasets also used in training, and how pseudo labels or SMPL fits are obtained. These omissions make it hard to judge reproducibility and fairness.

The comparison set is incomplete for several claims. Human3.6M trajectory evaluation only compares against TRAM, and the in-the-wild COCO point-cloud overlay is qualitative only. There is no quantitative evaluation of metric scale/body size, translation depth, or robustness to intrinsic-estimation errors in truly in-the-wild settings.

The method depends on UniDepth for images with unknown intrinsics, but the paper does not provide a sensitivity analysis to focal length/principal point errors or report failure modes beyond a brief limitation. This is important because metric translation can be highly sensitive to camera calibration quality.

Several baselines use temporal information or SLAM modules while the proposed method is per-frame; this is a strength, but the paper does not cleanly separate what is being evaluated: body recovery, root translation in camera coordinates, or world trajectory after external camera pose estimation. This blurs the interpretation of the global trajectory results.

Presentation and reproducibility need improvement: architecture details for the two ViTs and regressor are sparse, loss weights are omitted, data preprocessing/crop definitions are under-specified, and some text contains typos or imprecise phrasing. These are fixable, but currently they hinder independent replication.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: recovering human mesh, shape, and global translation at metric scale from monocular imagery, which is highly relevant for AR/VR, scene interaction, and motion analysis.

The central idea of conditioning HMR on perspective camera rays is simple and intuitively well motivated. Encoding intrinsics and crop/bounding-box geometry as a ray map is a plausible alternative to feeding raw camera parameters and box coordinates.

The paper includes useful discussion of why weak-perspective assumptions limit metric-scale recovery, and the ambiguity analysis in Sec. 3 helps frame what can and cannot be expected from monocular metric HMR.

The method is comparatively simple: it adds a ray encoder to an HMR-style regressor and does not require temporal input or an explicit trajectory module, which could make the approach practically attractive if validated more thoroughly.
The ablation in Table 5 suggests that the ray representation is much more effective than directly concatenating bounding-box and intrinsic parameters, especially on 3DPW.
weaknesses: The evidence does not support the paper's strongest claims. The abstract and conclusion claim state-of-the-art performance in local motion and global trajectory estimation, but Table 2 shows the method is worse than WHAM and TRAM on both 3DPW and EMDB-1 local pose/mesh metrics. Table 3 is also essentially tied with or slightly worse than TRAM under Masked-DROID, with only small gains under GT extrinsics. The claimed SOTA status is therefore overstated.

There is a serious reproducibility and evaluation concern: the implementation section says the model is trained on 3DPW, Human3.6M, and MPI-INF-3DPH, while the experiments evaluate on 3DPW and Human3.6M. The paper does not clearly specify train/test splits or how overlap is avoided. Without this, the reported 3DPW and Human3.6M results are difficult to interpret.

The claim that MetricHMR works without requiring any 3D information as training supervision is confusing and likely misleading. The model is trained on datasets that provide 3D annotations or fitted SMPL parameters, and the losses include pose mimic loss and shape loss. The paper later narrows the statement to no 3D joint loss, but this is materially different from no 3D supervision.

The camera-crop intrinsic formulation appears technically questionable. Eq. 4 writes terms such as (fx - ubbox)/s and cx/s, whereas standard crop-and-resize intrinsics would scale focal lengths and shift principal points, e.g. fx/s and (cx - ubbox)/s depending on the coordinate convention. If this is not merely a typesetting error, it undermines the core ray-map construction; if it is a typo, it is still consequential for reproducibility.

The evaluation is too narrow for the proposed metric-awareness claims. There is no systematic analysis of intrinsic-parameter noise, UniDepth failure modes, predicted versus ground-truth intrinsics, camera focal length variation, crop errors, human size variation, or out-of-distribution cameras. These are central to the paper's premise.

The in-the-wild COCO point-cloud overlay is only qualitative. It does not quantitatively validate metric shape or metric translation in unconstrained images, despite being used to support robustness and real-world accuracy claims.

The comparison set is incomplete for isolating the contribution. The paper needs stronger controlled baselines using the same HMR2.0 backbone and training data with alternative camera encodings, predicted intrinsics, CLIFF-style crop features, and possibly depth-conditioned variants. As written, it is hard to know whether gains come from the ray representation, training protocol, backbone, intrinsics, or dataset mixture.

The method depends on UniDepth when intrinsics are unknown, but latency, failure cases, and sensitivity to depth/intrinsic estimation errors are barely studied. The limitation section acknowledges this dependence in one sentence, which is insufficient given that this is essential for in-the-wild use.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence: there are typos and imprecise terms throughout, some metric definitions are unclear, the architecture lacks details needed for reimplementation, and the paper does not report runtime, parameter count, or exact backbone/ray encoder configuration in enough detail.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-addressed limitation of monocular HMR: recovering metric-scale body shape and camera-frame translation rather than only image-aligned meshes. The focus on standard perspective projection and camera intrinsics is well motivated and useful for downstream AR/VR, scene overlay, and trajectory estimation.

The camera-ray representation is a simple, technically plausible way to encode intrinsics and crop/bounding-box geometry in a form suitable for a neural regressor. The ablation in Table 5 is strong evidence that this representation matters: replacing it with direct Bbox+K conditioning severely degrades 3DPW performance.

The method is appealingly simple compared with trajectory-module or temporal pipelines. It estimates global translation from a single frame and remains competitive with stronger temporal/global baselines on EMDB-2 and Human3.6M trajectory metrics.

The paper includes a helpful analysis of metric ambiguity under perspective projection. It appropriately acknowledges that monocular metric HMR cannot yield a unique absolute solution and reframes the goal as recovering geometrically reasonable metric pose/shape/translation.
Experiments cover both local mesh recovery and global trajectory/motion estimation, with comparisons to relevant HMR and world-grounded methods such as CLIFF, WHAM, TRAM, TRACE, and GVHMR.
weaknesses: Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The paper states state-of-the-art performance broadly, but Table 2 shows the method is worse than WHAM and TRAM on local pose/mesh metrics, and Table 3 shows it is essentially tied with or slightly worse than TRAM under Masked-DROID for WA-MPJPE and W-MPJPE, with only small gains in ERVE or GT-extrinsic settings.

The dependence on camera intrinsics is central but not fully dissected. Results mix ground-truth intrinsics/camera poses and UniDepth-estimated intrinsics/depth, yet the paper does not provide enough sensitivity analysis to focal-length/principal-point errors or failure cases of UniDepth. This matters because the main benefit may degrade sharply under realistic in-the-wild camera calibration errors.

The supervision claim is potentially confusing. The paper says no 3D information is needed during training, but training uses datasets such as 3DPW, Human3.6M, and MPI-INF-3DHP and includes pose mimic and shape losses. The source of mimic targets and whether metric 3D annotations or pseudo-3D annotations indirectly supervise the system should be specified much more clearly.

The method section contains a likely incorrect or at least unreproducible crop intrinsic equation: Eq. 4 writes terms like (f_x - u_bbox)/s and c_x/s, whereas standard crop resizing would normally keep focal scaling separate from principal-point translation. Since the ray map is the core contribution, this ambiguity is material, not just presentation.

The ablation study is narrow. It mainly compares ray conditioning against direct Bbox+K input, but does not isolate ray encoder design choices, intrinsics noise, crop-size normalization, using predicted versus ground-truth intrinsics, or whether gains come from the representation versus increased model capacity.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The architecture sizes, ViT/backbone initialization, ray-map resolution/channels, loss weights, data preprocessing, pseudo-label generation, and exact train/evaluation splits are not described in enough detail to confidently reproduce the reported numbers.

The in-the-wild 3D overlay evidence is qualitative only. Figure 8 is visually promising, but there is no quantitative evaluation of metric scene alignment, point-cloud consistency, or robustness on images where UniDepth or person detection is inaccurate.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: metric human mesh recovery jointly with scene depth from a monocular image, moving beyond weak-perspective, image-aligned mesh recovery toward globally meaningful 3D placement.

The pixel-aligned camera-ray representation is a sensible way to encode intrinsics and crop/bounding-box effects, and the SynFocal experiment directly probes the focal-length sensitivity that motivates the method.

The method reports strong quantitative results across several established human mesh and trajectory benchmarks. In particular, the reported gains on 3DPW local pose, EMDB-2 global trajectory, and the synthetic varying-intrinsics setting support the claim that camera-aware conditioning helps metric localization.

The paper includes useful ablations showing that ray conditioning substantially improves global/trajectory metrics and that the MoE component gives additional gains. The routing visualizations also provide some qualitative evidence that experts specialize over body/background regions.

The human-guided depth refinement idea is practically useful: using metric human meshes as sparse scale anchors for monocular depth is plausible and yields reported improvements over MapAnything on the PROX split.
weaknesses: The central novelty is somewhat incremental. Camera/crop-aware human mesh recovery, perspective projection, metric depth priors, and MoE routing are all known ingredients; the contribution is mainly their combination rather than a clearly new formulation. The MoE design in particular is not deeply justified beyond generic expert specialization arguments.

The evidence for the Human MoE is not fully convincing. The main ablation shows a modest gain from '+ Ray' to '+ Ray & MoE' compared with the much larger gain from ray conditioning, and there is no detailed ablation of Patch MoE vs Global MoE, ray expert, shared expert, number of experts, load-balancing loss, or routing strategy.

The metric depth/scene recovery claim is under-evaluated. Depth refinement is tested only on a custom PROX 9:1 split, with limited baseline coverage and no cross-dataset evaluation. It is unclear how well the refinement generalizes beyond human-centric indoor RGB-D data or how sensitive it is to errors in the predicted mesh anchors.

Reproducibility is weak from the manuscript alone. Important details such as exact architecture dimensions, loss weights, data mixing ratios, preprocessing, intrinsic-estimation protocol, extrinsic handling, depth-refinement training details, and availability of SynFocal/code are either missing or deferred only partially to the supplement.

The global trajectory comparisons raise protocol questions. Some tables use predicted or GT extrinsics, but the proposed method is described as per-frame monocular recovery; the role of external camera/extrinsic estimation in world-frame trajectory evaluation is not sufficiently disentangled, which may affect fairness against video-based methods.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper claims state-of-the-art performance on both human mesh and scene recovery, but local pose results are mixed on EMDB-1, scene recovery is evaluated narrowly, and some comparisons omit relevant recent baselines or report missing metrics.

The synthetic SynFocal dataset is useful but insufficient as the primary evidence for robustness to varying intrinsics. Since it is generated from controlled assets and rendering, the result may not transfer to real zoom/focal-length variation without additional real-world validation.

Presentation quality needs improvement: there are many grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology, malformed equations/text extraction artifacts, and some unclear metric definitions. These do not invalidate the work, but they make it harder to assess the exact method and protocol.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: metric human mesh recovery with global 3D position and metric human-scene alignment from monocular input. The emphasis on camera intrinsics, crop-induced ambiguity, and bounding-box position is well motivated for moving beyond weak-perspective HMR.

The pixel-aligned camera ray representation is a sensible way to inject both intrinsics and crop geometry into a cropped-image HMR pipeline, and the reported ablation suggests it materially improves global position metrics over an image-only baseline.

The experimental section reports competitive numbers on several relevant benchmarks, including 3DPW, EMDB, and RICH. The method is especially strong among online/single-frame methods in the reported global trajectory tables, and it improves over the MapAnything depth baseline on the authors' PROX split.

The paper attempts to analyze the MoE routing behavior with patch/body-part heatmaps and global expert allocation plots, which is useful for interpreting whether the experts learn semantically differentiated roles.
weaknesses: The central claims are broader than the evidence supports. The title and abstract claim metric human mesh and scene recovery, but the scene/depth component is evaluated only on a PROX train/test split with a small table in the supplementary material. There is no broad evaluation on standard metric depth benchmarks, no clear cross-dataset generalization study, and no analysis of failure cases beyond a brief occlusion limitation.

Novelty is limited. Camera-ray conditioning, full-perspective HMR, monocular depth-based scaling, MoE routing, and using human priors for metric depth all have close precedents. The paper combines these ideas, but it does not convincingly establish that the combination is conceptually new enough or that MoE is the key reason for the gains.

The global trajectory evaluation is hard to interpret. The method is described as per-frame/single-image, yet tables compare against video/offline trajectory methods under predicted or ground-truth extrinsics. It is not sufficiently clear how camera extrinsics are obtained, whether temporal information enters through external systems, and whether all baselines use comparable camera inputs. This weakens the strongest quantitative claim.

The MoE evidence is not decisive. The ablation shows image-only, +ray, and +ray&MoE, but the MoE gain is modest relative to the ray gain. There is no comparison to a parameter-matched dense transformer, no expert-count sensitivity, no routing/loss ablation, and no runtime/parameter analysis. Thus the paper does not show that the added complexity is necessary.

The depth refinement module depends on the predicted mesh as sparse anchors and is trained on PROX, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze error propagation from inaccurate meshes, occlusions, contact regions, or incorrect intrinsics. The method may improve depth near humans while being much less reliable for general scene recovery, which is nevertheless claimed strongly.

Reproducibility is weak. Important details are missing or deferred: exact loss weights, training schedules for the depth module, dataset composition and filtering, how pseudo-GT is generated and used, SynFocal scale and splits, intrinsic/extrinsic estimation settings, and baseline reimplementation details. The proposed dataset is mentioned but not specified enough to judge its utility.

Some technical descriptions are internally inconsistent or under-specified. The MoE section first describes top-K routing but later says Soft MoE is used; the ray expert/shared expert interaction is not mathematically defined; the global MoE with a single query token is not clearly formulated; and the over-complete losses include coupled quantities such as height and SMPL shape without explaining why this does not introduce harmful supervision bias.

The writing and presentation contain numerous grammar issues and imprecise claims, but the more serious problem is scientific framing: terms such as 'state-of-the-art', 'metric', 'geometrically precise', and 'comprehensive' are used more strongly than the experiments justify.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: recovering human mesh, metric global position, and scene geometry from monocular images under realistic perspective camera assumptions. The motivation for using camera intrinsics and crop-aware camera rays is technically sound and well aligned with known weaknesses of weak-perspective HMR methods.

MetricHMSR is a coherent system contribution. Pixel-aligned camera ray maps explicitly encode focal length, principal point, crop, and scale information; the Human MoE architecture provides a plausible mechanism for separating patch-level and global-level visual factors; and the human-guided metric depth refinement module connects human mesh recovery to scene-scale reconstruction.

The empirical results are strong across several standard human recovery benchmarks. The method reports competitive or best performance on EMDB-2 global trajectory metrics, RICH root translation error, and 3DPW local pose metrics, while remaining an online/single-frame method compared with several offline video baselines.

The ablations support the main design choices. Adding ray information substantially improves global position estimates, and adding MoE gives further gains. The SynFocal experiment is also a useful diagnostic for robustness to focal-length variation, a setting that standard datasets often under-test.

The paper’s potential usefulness is high: a single-frame method that can produce metric human meshes and improved metric scene depth would be valuable for AR/VR, dataset pseudo-labeling, and human-scene understanding. The synthetic zoom-varying dataset is also a useful contribution if released.
weaknesses: Some claims about unified metric human and scene recovery are broader than the evidence. The scene-depth component is evaluated mainly on a PROX split, with additional depth results relegated to the supplement, while the main quantitative evidence focuses more heavily on human mesh and trajectory recovery than full human-scene reconstruction quality.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Important implementation details are underspecified, including exact loss weights, MoE/router settings beyond the high-level description, training schedules for the depth refinement module, use of estimated versus ground-truth intrinsics in each experiment, and details of the SynFocal dataset construction and splits.

The comparison protocol raises fairness questions. The model is trained on datasets including 3DPW and then evaluated on 3DPW, but the paper does not clearly state split handling or whether all baselines use comparable training data and intrinsics. The depth refinement evaluation uses a PROX train/test split created by the authors, which makes external comparison harder.

The technical novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental. Camera-aware conditioning, MoE routing, over-complete losses, and human-guided depth scale refinement each have precedents; the contribution is primarily in combining and adapting these ideas to metric HMSR rather than introducing a fundamentally new estimation principle.

The Human MoE component is not fully justified relative to its complexity. The reported MoE gain over ray-only is modest compared with the gain from camera rays, and there is limited analysis of compute cost, expert collapse, number of experts, or whether simpler capacity-matched transformer/MLP variants would achieve similar results.

The method depends on reliable human detection/cropping, SMPL fitting supervision, and either known or estimated camera intrinsics. Failure modes beyond heavy occlusion are not deeply analyzed, such as inaccurate intrinsics from VGGT/HumanFoV, unusual lenses, multi-person interactions, severe truncation, or cases where the human mesh prior is wrong and harms depth refinement.

The writing is understandable but has several presentation issues, including grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology, and occasional overstatement. These are mostly fixable, but the method and evaluation sections would benefit from more precise experiment bookkeeping.
